At page 3096 of the transcript, there was a discussion regarding the fact that in your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, you described Ljube Boskoski as an ultra-nationalist, and you confirmed that description in your testimony. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can I ask the Court Officer's assistance, please, to show us what is a video. It's Exhibit P278. I'm sorry, Your Honour, apparently it's our job to play this but we have to play it on the sanctioned system, so we will play it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, just so that you know, this particular video --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My microphone's on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This video was shot after the conflict. It was shot later on?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT (Resumed)
utterances.text: M'mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But I wanted to ask you, this comment that Mr. Boskoski makes about: "The only thing that can be condemned is treason," during your time in Macedonia and your research did you -- during 2001, did you have occasion to see or hear Mr. Boskoski make similar kinds of comments in public?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and afterwards one of the most vehement attacks Mr. Boskoski made was in January of 2002 against the head of the Macedonia-Helsinki Committee, herself an ethnic Macedonian, whom he accused twice on State Television of being State Enemy Number 1 and working contrary to the interests of the nation because she reported on some of the abuses committed against the ethnic Albanian community. And we issued a public letter to the President and to the Prime Minister expressing our concern for her and her safety. She was afraid to return to Macedonia because she feared arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, again, when you say "we," you're referring to --

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT (Resumed)
utterances.text: To the Human Rights Watch, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During your testimony, you clarified that paragraph 16 of your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor is written in a tone that is perhaps a bit too categorical and that your prior statements about Mr. Boskoski's involvement in the establishment and command of The Lions unit were based on media reports. This is at 3083 to 3084 of the transcript. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can, I'd like to show you an article. I don't believe this article is uploaded into e-court. It's from 65 ter number -- oh, it is uploaded. If we can see, please, what is 65 ter 136.1, please. I have some questions to ask you about this article. If we can't do this on e-court, I believe we have hard copies. If that's preferable for our assistance, that's fine. Perhaps a copy could be placed on the ELMO. Mr. Bouckaert, this is an article originally published in the English periodical "The Economist." It's dated 2nd of June, 2001. It's titled "NATO and the European Union Speak Peace. Macedonians Feel on the Edge of War." Could you look, please, at the very last paragraph on the first page. You need to look at the hard copy, Mr. Bouckaert, perhaps. I don't know if it's coming up on the ELMO. Yes, there it is. Mr. Bouckaert, I'm sorry, you can see it on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There's a paragraph that begins: "Mr. Trajkovski's ...," that's President Trajkovski's, "...room for manoeuvre is small, however. Last week's offensive was led by police units known as Tigers and backed by poorly-armed artillery and tanks, plus helicopters piloted by Ukrainians. If the Tigers had not been sent in, or so the President was warned by hard-line Slav Macedonians, then other feral creatures might have gone to work, including a group of ..." Can we turn to the next page, please. We need to see the top of the next page: " ... Including a group of toughs called The Lions who threatened to vent their wrath on ethnic Albanians in Skopje, the capital." Were these the kinds of press reports that you heard about this entity called the Lions in 2001, in the summer of 2001?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, this -- I know the person who wrote this report. I was in very close touch with him. He actually accompanied the Tigers on one of their operations, so he was very familiar with the security structures in Macedonia, and we met on an almost daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another newspaper article, Mr. Bouckaert, and again I have to bother our Court Usher. This is again from Exhibit 136. You refer to it as 136.2. It has ERN number N004-6244 to 6247. I won't read all of it to you. It's an article that begins at the bottom of the page N004-6244. It's an article originally published in the "Christian Science Monitor" on the 11th of September, 2001, by a journalist named Elizabeth Reuben. Mr. Bouckaert, did you know Elizabeth Reuben?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What can you tell us about her?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT (Resumed)
utterances.text: She's a very well-known journalist, and I've worked with her since 1998 or 1999, I've known her. She's considered one of the best investigative journalists out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This article is titled "A Simple NATO Mission Faces Bad-Faith and 'Lions'. Macedonian Paramilitaries Fill an Army Vacuum." If we can turn to the next page, please. We need to look at the top of the page. The first paragraph says: "A meeting nearly two weeks ago between NATO Secretary-General George Robertson and Macedonia's government leaders erupted into a verbal balance jousting match that has exposed just how tenuous NATO's mission is here and how easily the country will slip into war if NATO forces withdraw as planned in two weeks." In the next paragraph, we see this: "According to an official who attended the meeting, Lord Robertson accused Prime Minister Ljubce Georgievski and his Interior Minister, Ljube Boskoski, of building up paramilitary forces that threaten the safety of his troops. The Prime Minister lashed back accusing NATO of having a secret agenda here." And then later on we see a sentence: "The Prime Minister threatened to walk out, and Mr. Boskoski, a former sweetshop owner and member of the special forces in Croatia, exploded, telling Robertson that he and his aide should be declared persona non grata in Macedonia, and NATO should be sent to The Hague." Do you see that, Mr. Bouckaert?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Two paragraphs later, we see this: "What's clear on the ground here is that Boskoski does have special forces he has prepared to exploit that vacuum. They're called The Lions, which is the symbol of the ruling VMRO Party. And they've been training at the Centre for Strategic Studies on the outskirts of Skopje. As one moderate Macedonian security official in the government said, Boskoski has threatened to use them 'to clear the terrain on the Sar mountains' where the villages of Albanian rebels-turned-civilians are concentrated." Four paragraphs below, we see the following: "The problem, says a NATO official, is that they," referring to the so-called Lions, "are totally outside the chain of command, pursuing Boskoski's own agenda, and even the police general has no control over them." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Again, were these the kind of press reports that you were receiving and reviewing during the summer of 2001?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and I should say that Elizabeth Reuben has excellent contacts within the US government and within NATO, so I have no doubt who -- I have no doubt about the credibility of her sourcing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, at page 3159 of the transcript, you explained to my colleague that the Macedonian government, after the 12th of August, made general statements that the people in Ljuboten were terrorists; however, the government presented no evidence of that claim. In your experience, what was typically the conduct of Macedonian government officials when they announced publicly about operations that had been carried out against terrorists?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the ordinary course of events, there would be a press conference where they would display the weapons that were captured, any propaganda, flags, uniforms, or other NLA materials that were found to show that they had actually carried out a raid against the NLA. They did so after an August 5th event in Skopje itself, in which five members of the NLA were killed under, let's say, questionable circumstances. They displayed a large cache of arms on television that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did they ever display, so to speak, captured NLA soldiers or terrorists?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall ever seeing any so-called terrorists, any of the people who had been detained at the village of Ljuboten on the 12th of August, displayed or shown on television?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT (Resumed)
utterances.text: I saw some footage related to people fleeing from the village, some video footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. But not of --

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT (Resumed)
utterances.text: But not of people in detention, no. And I was actively looking for that kind of footage because I had spoken to some of the relatives who had visited people who had been detained from Ljuboten and spoke about obvious bruises and signs of beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned this killing of Commander Teli and some other persons on 5th of August, 2001. I would like to show you a bit more sir video material, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is another clip from 65 ter 305 --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Before the video clip is shown, I would like a clarification on the part of Mr. Saxon whether he intends to show material which relate to the Teli incident. It's not a matter that we've raised with the witness on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is a matter that has come up during cross-examination, because this witness talked, at page 3159, about the usual practice of the government was that -- excuse me. He said that: "Macedonian government made general statements that people in Ljuboten were terrorists, but presented no evidence of that." So this is the issue I'm trying to explore with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, the first thing we notice is that the picture relating to that particular incident was shown to the witness in examination-in-chief. If the Prosecution had intended to explore that matter, it should have done that at this stage. Furthermore, we asked no question of the witness in particular in relation to that incident, and as far as we can see it is irrelevant to the charges in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Try again, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not aware that I showed a picture to this witness in examination-in-chief related to this incident on August 5th. That's the first point. My memory is not always perfect, I'm the first to admit that, but I'm not aware that I did that. It may be true that on cross-examination my colleague asked no questions about this particular incident. However, the questions that my colleague did ask elicited a response, an information, that in the Prosecution's submission is worthy of clarification, and that is simply the essential purpose of redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can show the clip from 65 ter Exhibit 305. It begins at 11 seconds and goes to 2 minutes and 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this is being played without sound, Your Honour. It was broadcast on Macedonian Television after the 5th of August, 2001. We see what appears to be a camouflage uniform with the word "Teli" written on it. We see some packages that have the words "Explosives" written on it, a number of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Parts of weapons. We see what appear to be automatic rifles and then automatic handguns. A cellular phone. We see some, it looks like, camouflage rucksacks, and again more automatic rifles. If we could stop here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is this the video material that you saw broadcast on Macedonian Television after this incident on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you saw -- how can I phrase this question? Again, the fact that you saw no such presentation after the 12th of August, what conclusions, if any, did you draw from that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT (Resumed)
utterances.text: It added to my evaluation that there was no such evidence available for the government to show.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender that last video clip, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll reiterate the objection as to the relevance. We think it is typically the sort of material that falls under Rule 89(D) and Rule 95 [realtime transcript read in error"92(5)"]. It has absolutely no relevance to the charges and this witness, insofar as the evidence is concerned, has given his view that this material was relevant to his belief that there had been no terrorists in the village. However, the material itself has absolutely no relevance to the charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be admitted. Oh, I'm sorry. Before we act, Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may ask the witness to indicate, where was this video clip shot? Does he know the location of this house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I indicated in my direct testimony, I visited this house on the day after the incident, and we also concluded at that time that the government version, that these men had died during a fierce gun battle, was inconsistent with the evidence we found at the scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're in the process of receiving the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P364, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And it's received for the fact that it was a basis for an opinion of the witness about a fact that is not central to the case against the accused on this indictment so that Mr. Mettraux and Mr. Apostolski are aware that the Chamber well appreciates the distinction they make and the objection that is raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour, and if I may correct the transcript. At line 15 of page 58, it was Rule 95 that was referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness. I do have some -- I would like to tender some documents, but I don't know the witness needs to be here for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in -- for the sake of propriety, the comment of my learned colleague Mettraux, referring to the direct examination of our colleague Saxon, was directly based on my suggestion because I thought that Mr. Saxon has asked this question to the witness -- of the witness in direct examination. I was not able to verify whether my suggestion was appropriate, and if someone had made a mistake, it was me, and I apologise, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is most gracious of you, Ms. Residovic. Thank you. Mr. Bouckaert, you'll be pleased to learn that that concludes the questioning of you in this case. The Chamber would thank you indeed for your attendance in The Hague, for the assistance you've been able to give, and the time that you have, in the end, been able to spare to enable your evidence to be concluded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm glad to have been of assistance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and of course you may now return to your other activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were two documents that had been marked for identification a week or so ago, and I mentioned them yesterday. They were Exhibits P303 and P304, and my colleague indicated that he had no objection that they be admitted into evidence at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, what we would like to specify in relation to yesterday's comments about P303 and P304, I understand Mr. Saxon is referring to the reports of Mr. Kostadinov and Kopacev. What we would like to specify is we've indicated that we have no objection to the admission, however, the Defence will certainly challenge the reliability or may, in any case, challenge the reliability of some of the statements made within those documents. The objection may be taken at a later stage, and we still believe it is preferable that the admission or the decision on the admission of the documents be postponed until Mr. Kostadinov, who is the author of one of those two documents, appears as a witness for the Prosecution. At this stage, the Defence believes, will be the time to determine whether the content of those documents in part or in their totality are, indeed, reliable and, as such, are admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object to having this written document submitted into evidence on the basis that neither the first nor the second witness have authenticated the accuracy of the text. They did not authenticate the veracity of the text contained in those written documents, and it is for these reasons that I propose that they are not admitted by the Court in evidence. When the witness comes, the witness who is the author of the text, I think that would be the right time for the documents to be tendered and admitted into evidence in case he verifies them as being authentic and accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems to the Prosecution, with great respect, that the Defence is trying to have its cake and eat it too. It used both of these documents yesterday on cross-examination to make points for its own case, and so it seems, at the very least, contradictory, to now say it is not -- the time has not yet come to admit these documents into evidence. With respect to the creators of the documents, one of the creators, Mr. Kopacev, will not be coming. He is not on the Prosecution's witness list. We don't intend to call him. The other one, Mr. Kostadinov, will be called as a witness. However, we have already had large portions of these documents authenticated not only by Mitre Despodov but now further supported on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think we need to continue the debate backwards and forwards, gentlemen. Could the Chamber indicate that both documents will be received. They were not received yesterday on a very simple procedural point. We were in the middle of cross-examination, and the documents were referred to and relied upon. Mr. Saxon got to his feet then and sought to tender them. The Chamber was simply keeping him to his proper time for doing that, which was re-examination. The conditions for their admission, in the view of the Chamber, having been satisfied at that point, accordingly, therefore, the two are received as exhibits. And that does not mean, of course, that subsequent cross-examination of other witnesses about their content will not be taken into account in assessing what weight, if anything, would be given to them. Now, Mr. Saxon, is there more?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm grateful for the Chamber keeping the Prosecution honest, so to speak, in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have a limited sight merely in procedural order, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Prosecution would also seek to tender what has been marked for identification P352, which was the report which Mr. Bouckaert drafted for Human Rights Watch, and I hope I have the number correct, the press release disseminated by Human Rights Watch regarding that report that has -- has been marked for identification P353. We seek to tender those at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the leave of the Chamber, we at first make a very very short comment in response to Mr. Saxon's suggestion of a cake and the desire to eat it as well. The only portion which the Defence relied upon in the two documents in questions were the part which related to the conversation relevant between the President and other individuals, Mr. Despodov in particular, and the Defence relied on that document because it had been properly corroborated by other evidence which we also put to the witness. The Defence did not intend at this stage to rely on any other parts of these documents. That is the first thing we would like to underline. The second matter, as pertaining to the report of Mr. Bouckaert or Human Rights Watch, we obviously object strongly to the admission of these documents under Article 21 of the Statute and Rule 89 and 95 of the Rules. We submit that there are a number of very serious shortcomings in this report which renders it unreliable. All of these matters have been explored by the Defence with the witness. Many of those have not been explored by the Prosecution in re-examination. I will list them in no particular order, Your Honour. The first one concerns the issue of the translation of the information which was provided by villagers or otherwise to Mr. Bouckaert. Mr. Bouckaert has indicated that he was unable to verify the accuracy of the information which was given to him independently. The interviews were not recorded, whether video, audio or otherwise. No proper statements were taken. The information provided by the witnesses were not adopted, they were not signed. The information was taken, we understand, in summary fashion in notes taken by Mr. Bouckaert, to which the Prosecution has not sought formally to obtain access. These notes have not been produced. The accuracy of the reporting within these notes have not been established. The accuracy of the summary of these notes, which have then been made into the reports, has not been established. There's also a rule which is the rule of best evidence which applies in this Tribunal. We understand it does not necessarily apply to its extreme limits and perhaps shouldn't be. However, the Prosecution has taken the view not to call many of the individuals which are listed by Mr. Bouckaert in his reports as source of information and which, on the face of it, were available to give evidence before this Tribunal. A further matter is the inability of the Defence to test the reliability and credibility of many of the individuals who have given evidence or given information to Mr. Bouckaert. We have only been able to challenge the accuracy or the reliability of the method and methodology which Mr. Bouckaert has used. We also have the matter pertaining to the reliability of the evidence, and the Defence submits that it has established that some of the information provided to Mr. Bouckaert, to the extent that it could be tested by material in the possession of the Defence, is unreliable, it contradicts some of the statements given to the Prosecution office, it also contradicts evidence which was given before this Tribunal. It's not simply a matter of weight, we submit, Your Honour, as the Prosecution would surely submit. The main and principal problem for the Defence would be its inability to test the actual information, the basis for Mr. Bouckaert's conclusion; that is, the evidence on which he relied to come to its conclusion. We've also underlined during the cross-examination of the witness and during the exercise of putting that proposition to this witness, that much of its information, of the information contained in the report, was uncorroborated. Furthermore, we understand that the evidence, and the witness has conceded, was not admitted in compliance with local laws, since there was no presence of an authorised official which would render it inadmissible in local court. This last matter may not be highly relevant to the Tribunal, however it is a matter, we submit, of some weight. We finally indicate this: That we haven't made a direct attack on the honesty of this witness and do not wish to do so in his absence. However, we believe that this investigation was made in a rush, that it was one-sided. We have said it was a one-week investigation conducted by one man, where most of the evidence, as pointed out to him, had been taken by one side without taking any steps to verify many of the allegations made by him, in particular, very serious allegations against Mr. Boskoski.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the interpreters ask you to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, the interpreters will be happy to understand that I'm almost finished, simply to indicate, Your Honour, the legal basis for our submissions Article 21 of the Statute and Rule 89 and 95 of the Rules; thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mettraux. Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I fully support the objection made by my colleague in relation to the admission of this evidence, and I also wish to stress that this is a one-side view of the events primarily in relation to the interviewing of persons. No statements were taken from the both entities that make up that -- the population of that village, who live there. I furthermore think that by not asking for reports from the legitimate institutions of the Republic of Macedonia, and here I primarily refer to the prosecutor's office and the Court, I think that the report is one-sided, and in this sense I think that it should not be admitted into evidence. And regarding all the other issues, I fully support the statement made by my colleague Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the view of the Chamber, the report, and the press release will be received. We would observe that the issue of the quality of the content of the investigation, so-called, which is reflected in much of the report has been very extensively tested, and it has been tested in a way which has exposed quite glaringly a number of aspects about the procedure and the results which clearly will tell in respect of the weight that can be attached to some parts of the report. But the report covers a very wide range of material, both of factual events and, in a sense, historical matters, and the relevance and weight of those various parts does vary quite a deal. And in some respects, the report is clearly of relevance and valuable. In other respects, while its content are relevant for the reasons that have been tested so carefully in cross-examination and re-examination, the question of the weight that can be attached to them is one that is very open indeed at this stage. The procedure, in a tribunal such as this, of receiving reports from agencies of standing and attempts at independence is one that is well established. It does not follow that because a report is received, that the Chamber accepts the content and the result of the report. The Chamber looks to the direct evidence. There has been quite a body of that, about matters dealt with in the report, and the Chamber, as I'm sure counsel appreciate, is simply not going to pick up a report and treat its content and its conclusions as established facts. They are merely a part of the extensive material which Chamber must take into account. And Mr. Mettraux's submission, that here was a hasty report prepared in only a week or so, underlines the comment I've just made because this Chamber will not be able to spend just a week in assessing the facts of this case. It is clear it is going to spend something in the order of six months or more hearing detailed evidence, and it is upon that evidence primarily and not on this or similar reports that conclusions will be reached by this Chamber. So if the Registrar could note, then, that those two documents which were marked for identification will now become exhibits. Mr. Saxon, is there anything more?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There is another witness, Your Honour, but not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at the time before we must have our break, and clearly the witness should wait until after the break. I was wondering whether there was anything more of a procedural nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour, only that Ms. Motoike will lead the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a relatively short application which we would like to make at this stage in relation to the calling of Mr. Ostreni. I simply do not know whether Your Honour would wish to do so at this stage, or perhaps after the break, or tomorrow, or at your convenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I suspect it will take longer more than the tapes would allow, so we must hear you after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now, and we resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There are two matters in relation to which we would wish to be heard at this stage. The first one concerns the evidence of Mr. Ostreni or, rather, the timing thereof. It's an application we make with some reluctance, but we believe we have to make it and to make it at this stage. The Defence has made a number of applications for assistance to a number of state or entities for the provision of material which we believe to be relevant and important in relation to this particular witness and a number of other witnesses in this case. At this stage, two of these requests, we understand, are being processed or are in the process of being fulfilled by the two states in question. Two of the other applications are unfortunately not even there, at this stage. One of the applications has simply been ignored, if I may put it in those terms, and the Defence intend to make a further application with the Trial Chamber in relation to this one. As for the fourth application, we also intend to make a further application with the Trial Chamber because of what we believe to be an incomplete or inappropriate effort on the part of the state in question to provide the Defence with the material that is relevant to this matter. We believe that should we be asked or expected to proceed with the cross-examination of this witness on the 15th, the Defence could be either prejudiced by the absence of this material, which we have requested, or, in any case, we might not even be in a position to go for very long with the cross-examination, which may be good news to the completion strategy, but we believe that this would put the Defence in the position of having to do a very short cross-examination and then reserve its right to call this witness again for further cross-examination once the material come in our possession. We believe that this is an inefficient use of resources and that the Defence, the Prosecution, and, we hope, the Tribunal resources will be much better used if the evidence of that particular witness were postponed until we receive those documents. We highlight also the fact that this witness is called solely for the purpose of cross-examination, his statement having been tendered pursuant to Rule 92 bis. We also explain our reluctance, Your Honour, to do this application because of the fact that we understand that this may have consequences for the Prosecution, for the Trial Chamber, for the Registry, for VWS, for the witnesses, for the witness himself, and we can express our understanding that this application may cause some disruption and some problem. We believe, however, that it is sufficiently important to justify the postponement of the evidence of this witness. And perhaps, Your Honour, while I'm on my feet, so that perhaps Mr. Saxon can answer both matters at the same time, the second application or the second submissions concern an application by the Defence for Mr. Tarculovski concerning a suggested on-site visit to Ljuboten. We wish simply to indicate that we support the application of the Tarculovski Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Apostolski, is there anything that you would wish to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I support the statement by my colleague Mettraux again, only mentioning that the Prosecutor's Office has given us a large volume of material just a few weeks ago, 5.000 pages related to NLA, Your Honour, so we believe that we need more time to analyse that voluminous material and in relation to the cross-examination of the witness. It might be a mistake on our part, that we haven't analysed that material thus far, but still we believe that if it does not create problems for the Prosecution, the evidence by this witness should be postponed and he should be physically present here in this court after the summer recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Apostolski. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can respond, first of all, to the information just provided by my colleague Mr. Apostolski. It is generally correct that several weeks ago, perhaps a month, that the Prosecution provided thousands of pages of material related to the NLA to the Defence. However, there's quite a bit of context to this. First of all, this disclosure was performed pursuant to a specific request from the Defence, not because the Prosecution felt that all this material was relevant under 66(B) or fell within the scope of Rule 68. Indeed, the Prosecution specifically informed the Defence, before any disclosure was made, that it might want to come to the office of the OTP and review the material first before making a decision to receive such a voluminous amount of material, and that indeed was what happened several weeks ago. The Office of the Prosecutor made its staff and its resources available to do that, and it was at that time that the members of the Defence at that time decided, instead of taking only portions of this voluminous amount of material, that they would simply take the entire thing and review it as they saw fit. So this related disclosure, Your Honour, should not have any bearing on whether the video link of Mr. Ostreni is postponed or not. With respect to the application made by Mr. Mettraux, the Prosecution is sympathetic to the difficulties that the Defence are having with their requests for more information. Having said that, I feel it's my obligation to explain to the Chamber as well the difficulties that have become painfully and personally aware to me during the last few weeks as we have struggled to set up the video link that is currently scheduled. A video link conference in the United Nations headquarters in New York City requires the technical capabilities and organisational capabilities of members of the Registry, particularly the section called ITSS. It requires the work of the Court Officer. It requires the work of members of the Prosecution. It also requires the work of a significant number of people at United Nations headquarters in New York, work that has already been performed to arrange the video link that is presently scheduled to begin on the 16th of July, and I simply cannot tell the Chamber at this point how easy or how difficult it will be to reschedule another video link. There are rooms -- a limited number of rooms and a limited number of amount of equipment at United Nations headquarters that make such video links -- video conferencing available. However, there is also great demand for these rooms and this equipment and for the technicians, and they are often, as they are this month, fully booked. I simply need to inform the Chamber of that. I also do not know, Your Honours, the availability of the witness if we try to reschedule the video link. The witness has been gracious enough to make the entire week of the 16th of July open. He will be available for the currently-scheduled video link testimony. But I simply can't make an affirmation to the Trial Chamber at this point about his ongoing availability and whether it will be at a time that is convenient for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, I'm trying to remember, but do not clearly remember, the situation of the witness. He was to be in the United States for a period, but was he not then returning to his normal place of living in the region?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is my understanding of the witness's plans, and again I have not spoken to him via telephone in some months now, but it was my understanding that the witness was planning to spend at least three months in the United States. However -- however, the witness's intent was, if it were possible for him to extend his visa and stay longer, he intended to do so. That was my understanding, Your Honour, when we discussed this matter I guess it was in April. I can't tell you now what the witness's current plans are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, unless he gets an extension of his visa, he will need to be out in three months. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is my understanding, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When did those three months commence, Mr. Saxon? Are you able to tell us that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm deeply afraid I'm about to give misinformation, but it's my recollection that Mr. Ostreni travelled from Macedonia to the United States around the 25th or 26th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The view of the Chamber commences from the fact that we sought to accommodate the personal travel plans of this Prosecution witness, when it was his expectation that he would be spending three months in the United States holding only a single entry visa, which meant that he could not have come to The Hague in the course of that three months because he would not then be able to re-enter the United States, and to try and meet that exigency, the Chamber was prepared to entertain a video link with to the United States so that it would hear and see the witness give his evidence with the witness being in the United States, counsel and the Chamber being here. Quite distinctly from that, there have been efforts by the Defence for Mr. Boskoski to obtain information relevant to its cross-examination of that witness from various governments and a government organisation in Europe. Mr. Mettraux advises, in short summary, that at the moment they have not been sufficiently successful in getting responses from those requests, even though there have been orders by the Chamber in respect of them, such that the Defence of Mr. Boskoski would not be in a position to complete, even if it could begin, a cross-examination of the witness during the video link which is planned for the week after next. In those circumstances, given the complications of the procedures involved, it seems to the Chamber that the most practical course at this time is to abandon the plans for a video link from New York during the week after next. That means that the evidence of this witness will not be able to be heard until after the court vacation. When the witness will be heard will be a matter for liaison between the Victims and Witnesses Unit and the Prosecution. Obviously, there will be some consultation with the Boskoski Defence as well to ensure that they have reached a position of being ready, and it will then be a question whether the witness is still in the United States or has returned to his home country. If the latter, there would seem to be no particular difficulty about the witness giving evidence here. If the witness is in the United States, then despite Mr. Apostolski's submissions, the Chamber would remain with the view that the evidence should be heard via video link. That position having been reached, we must ask Mr. Saxon, of course, to then look again at his list of witnesses, undo the arrangements that have been made tentatively for the video link, and look at witnesses during the week after next.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour, we'll do that. Your Honour, my colleague raised one more matter, a motion for a site visit, and just if I can tell the Chamber very briefly. The Prosecution does not intend to object to this motion. However, the Prosecution wishes to respond in writing because there are certain portions of the proposed -- of the proposal that we wish to comment on quite carefully, so we will do that in writing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I say, Mr. Saxon, that the Chamber has received the motion and is well aware of it and the arguments put in support of it, but approaches the proposal with caution at this stage. We do not lightly undertake site visits and have only ever done so once in the course of -- this is now the fourth trial we have sat together so that the need for a site visit, given that it involves delay, it involves big administrative problems and cost, the need will have to be demonstrated quite clearly by the arguments advanced by the parties, and the Chamber would need to be persuaded not only of need but that a visit will make a significant difference to its consideration of the case. So be aware that the job lies ahead of the parties, if they want to persuade the Chamber that there is adequate justification for that. At a point earlier today, Mr. Saxon, a discussion between the Judges included the possibility we might ask of you how you saw now the completion date for the Prosecution case. In view of what has happened today, I think it would be asking you to look into a very obscure crystal ball to try and make a guess at the moment, unless you have something you would like to volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I think it would be, quite frankly, more appropriate for the Prosecution to ponder the matter at least overnight before making any response, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is constantly looking at the question of how to plan the continuation of this hearing and other matters that go with it, and of course if it were to come to a site visit, when and how best to manage that, so that we are trying to get these things within a time scale to assist our planning. So if you could ponder, we would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Prosecution will ponder, Your Honour, and may I say so, I hope the Trial Chamber is in receipt of a proposal to speed up the trial process which the Prosecution sent last night. Of course, the reaction of the parties and the Chamber to this proposal would obviously have an impact about time estimates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: True, but the starting point of the problem, as I think we have sought to underline, is the time taken by the Prosecution with each witness, which generally exceeds the time allowed in total for the witness. So the remedy could be shorter and simpler in adopting straightened rules. Well, with those matters dealt with, we, I hope, now can turn to Ms. Motoike's witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon. The Prosecution at this time would call Mario Jurisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good evening, sir. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [The witness answers through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Motoike has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Good evening, sir. Is your name Mario Jurisic?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And in August 2001, were you a lieutenant commander of the 2nd Infantry Company with the 3rd Battalion, 1st Guardist Brigade with the Army of the Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Had you been assigned to this particular command since July 2001, at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And as a commander during this particular period of time, that is, in 2001, did you have occasions to see orders issued by the President of the Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Have you seen orders issued by the President of the Republic of Macedonia at any time during your course of being in the army?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Are you still an active member of the Army of the Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And what is your position now?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: I am now in the Chiefs of Staff of the Army of the Republic of Macedonia, and I deal with personal management issues, development -- professional development of all military and civil persons in the Army of the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: If I could draw your attention back to August of 2001 for a moment. MS.MOTOIKE: Your Honours, with the assistance of the usher, we have binders with the exhibits I'd like to show this particular witness. If we could please display what's already been admitted as P00298. It's tab 1 of today's binders. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Mr. Jurisic, do you see the map that is displayed before you? It has some coloured markings on it. Do you recognise this particular map?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: I'm drawing your attention to a signature, what looks to be a signature under the words -- it says "Map 2" in English. There's a signature in there in the upper-left corner. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Forgive me, Your Honours, but I see "Map 2" in front of me. Is it the same map in question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Yes. Does this assist you, Mr. Jurisic? It is the map you're looking at in hard copy form.

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And, again, drawing your attention back to August of 2001, are the positions of the 2nd Infantry Company that you commanded indicated on this particular map?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And if I can draw your attention, there are -- I know that this is -- appears in English. There are names of particular locations that are on the upper margin of this particular map, and one of them says "Smuk," and I believe that should say "Smok," S-m-o-k; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can see it's written "Smuk," it should be "Smok."

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And there's also a position named Bomba, and further to the right there is a position named Maka, Volk and Oril, and Jastreb. Do you see those?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see them, with a slight correction, if I may. This is not Maka, this is Mecka.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And just so that we get the spelling correct, how should that be spelled?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: M-e-c-k-a.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you. And these particular points that I've referred you to, are those the observations points for your particular company, that is, the 2nd Company?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And there's also a name above in the middle of the document of the map. It says" Zevro" [phoen]. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Is that a mortar battery position within your battalion?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And in 2001, particularly in August of 2001, was your battalion comprised of three companies, with the fourth element being this mortar battery company named Zevro?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And if I could show you a photograph --?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: If we could please display it, it's 65 ter 199.28, which is tab 5 of today's binders.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Mr. Jurisic, you see the photo that's displayed before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And do you recognise what is depicted in this particular photograph?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Is this photograph taken from the position that you referred to as Smok?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Is it taken from the position called Bomba?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And is the village of Ljuboten visible in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: If you could, with the assistance of the usher, would you please mark the area of the photo where you see Ljuboten village, please?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And you've marked that with a rectangular -- loose rectangular figure on the photo. Mr. Jurisic, is the entire village of Ljuboten visible from this particular position?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be tendered, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P365, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And Mr. Jurisic, I would like to please show you another photograph so that we can get a visual of some of the locations you've indicated on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Can we please show N006-7603. It is not in the binder for today because it is actually in the court binder for this particular case. It's page 5. It's N006-7603 is the ERN. I'm sorry, it might be my fault. It's N005-7603. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Mr. Jurisic, do you recognise what's depicted in this particular photo that's displayed on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And basically the photo is a shot of Ljuboten village with a mountain range in the far background. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And if you could, please, tell us whether or not there are any of your positions of your company that are visible along this mountain range that is depicted in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And with the assistance of the usher, could you please mark for us the locations or the positions that your 2nd Company had that are visible in this particular photograph?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Now, the circle that you made in the top there, that's to the far right, can we number that with a "1", please.

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Let's start with the "1" to the left, then. So the position marked with a "1", is that position the Bomba or the Smok position?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: This is Smok.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And if you could, please, the circle in the middle that you've marked, could you mark that with a number "2", please.

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And could you tell us what position that is, the number "2" indicates?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: This is Bomba.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And the circle on the far right, could you number that with a "3", please.

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And could you also tell us what that position that's marked as a number "3", what is that -- the name of that position?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: This is Mecka.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we tender this, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Just some general questions, Mr. Jurisic, about your particular battalion in August of 2001. Was the commander of your battalion Major Mitre Despodov?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And who was your commander in August of 2001?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Major Mitre Despodov was head of my battalion and of my company, I was the head of my company.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. So Major Despodov was the commander of your battalion in 2001?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will receive the exhibit number while that is being considered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P366, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Major Jurisic, Major Despodov then went to the commander of the battalion that your company fell within in 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes, the commander of my battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And was the command of your battalion in Ljubanci?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Well, did your battalion have a command headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Was it located in the village of Ljubanci?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And did your command also have an -- not your company command but the battalion command, also have an operational and logistics headquarters in Ljubanci?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Was the operational headquarters based in the Ljubanci School building?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: If I could show you another photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: If we could show, please, 65 ter 199.25. This is tab 6, and actually it is also Photo B, page 7 of the court binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Mr. Jurisic, do you see the photograph that's displayed before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And does this photograph depict the Ljubanci School building where the operational headquarters for your battalion were?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we tender this, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P367, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Jurisic, did the battalion also have a logistics headquarters that was located at the Children's Rest House?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you can state the questions more precise. Logistics headquarters, what does that mean, in fact, what does it entail?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: I can rephrase. I apologise, Mr. Jurisic. What I was asking was: You had indicated that your battalion had a logistics headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: I guess what I was asking was: Is the logistics headquarters that you refer to, is that located at the Children's Rest House?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Was it located at the Children's Rest House in August of 2001?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And where was the logistics headquarters, then, located at in 2001?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: In the school building.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: The school building that is still depicted before you on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: If I could show you -- sorry. If I could show you another photograph, which is 65 ter 199.26. It is tab 7 of today's binders. It's also photo A, page 7 of the court binder. Do you see this particular photograph, Mr. Jurisic?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And could you tell us, these buildings that are located in the upper right corner of this particular photograph, do you recognise what those buildings are?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the rest house.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And could you tell us, in August of 2001, what was this rest house used for by your company?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: The rest house housed my company, which means that the whole rest for my company, when they were not on duty, was carried out in this rest house. Food was prepared here, showers were taken here, personal hygiene and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And was it also the same with respect to the other companies of your battalion; that is, did the other persons in other companies of your battalion also have access to this rest house?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we tender this, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before we do, we did receive tab 6 as Exhibit P367, but it is already Exhibit P233.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: I am being handed a note as to that, Your Honour, yes. Thank you for that. I didn't realise it was already P233. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That being so it will not become Exhibit P367.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And we now turn to tab 7.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P367, Your Honours, for the document bearing 65 ter number 199.26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Mr. Jurisic, if I could draw your attention to a particular day, which is Saturday, 11 August of 2001. Were you on duty that particular day?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And do you recall if you saw your -- the commander, which is Mitre Despodov, at any time that day?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And did you, at some point on that morning of Saturday, did you receive any orders or requests from Commander Despodov?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what those orders or requests were?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: The orders which I received from my commander were to prepare the positions from possible attacks, additional attacks by terrorists, that is to say, maximum engagement. As far as I recall, further establishing the -- putting up the personnel who came to the unit, finishing their training, the soldiers who came to join the unit, to increase their combat readiness of the company. And I also -- it was made -- it was told to me by the commander about an order from the President for maximum combat readiness in my part of the defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: At some point do you recall if you were at the Children's Rest House on that Saturday?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: This Saturday, yes, I was there in the rest house, but it depends on which part of the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Well, at any time at the Children's Rest House on that day, at any time did persons come to that location?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Could you tell us who these persons were?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: They were police officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And what were these police officers wearing?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Regular equipment which they usually wear.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Were they wearing any type of uniform or dress?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were in camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Did they have any insignia on their camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes, they had the police emblems.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Do you recall about how many of these police officers you saw at the Children's Rest House that day?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: At this moment, I cannot recall the exact number, but somewhere around ten persons. I truly cannot say the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Do you recall whether these policemen were equipped with weapons?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes, standard weapons worn by the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And at the time when you saw them, had they already been equipped with these weapons?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And when you say "standard weapons worn by the police," could you be more specific? What kind of weapons did you see that they had?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: They had automatic guns, pistols. At this moment, I cannot concretely remember whether they had snipers or something similar, but what does remain in my memory are pistols, automatic rifles. At the moment, this is what I can recollect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Do you know what a Zolja is?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Do you recall if any of these policemen were equipped with Zoljas?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Were they equipped with bulletproof vests; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were wearing them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And do you recall when these policemen arrived at the Children's Rest House?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: I believe it was somewhere in the evening, sometime in the evening, at dusk.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Do you recall how these persons arrived at the Children's Rest House?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And how did they arrive?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: They arrived in one police vehicle. When I say "police vehicle," I mean a police car.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Was it just one car or were there several?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: One vehicle and one truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Do you recall if you received any orders from Commander Despodov with respect to these policemen?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: At this moment, I cannot recall whether I was told in person or by phone or in a command line by the liaison officers, but I do know that I was informed that such people were coming to the rest house.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Were you informed as to what these people were going to do at the rest house?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: I was not informed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: While these policemen were at the Children's Rest House, were they under your authority?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: They were not under my command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Were you given any other orders by Commander Despodov with respect to any mortars on Saturday, 11 August 2001?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is part of the main order for increasing the maximum combat readiness, which also means the positioning of the mortars.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Going back to the policemen at the Children's Rest House, do you recall the identity of any of these policemen?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, who it is that you can remember as far as the policemen that were there?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: The person who collected the food.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And can you describe this person who collected the food?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Average height, black hair, this is so. I don't remember the colour of his eyes or any particular distinctions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And when you say "collecting the food," do you mean collecting the food that was served at the rest house?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Do you recall being interviewed by representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor on 9 November 2004?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And during that interview, do you recall being shown two photo-boards of persons?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And prior to being shown these particular photo-boards, do you recall if you were given certain advisements with respect to the photo lines that you were going to be presented with?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: I did not understand the question. Can you please make it more precise?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Do you recall being advised of anything prior to being shown these two photo-boards during your interview with the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And do you remember what that advisement was?

utterances.speaker: MARIO JURISIC
utterances.text: To point to a person if I -- if I am sure that I had seen that person before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I sense what you're about to do, and it's clearly going to take more time than we have. So I think we should adjourn now, and we resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but we must interrupt your evidence now, to resume in the morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
